{{Short description|Ordinals in mathematics and set theory}}
In the mathematical discipline of [[set theory]], there are many ways of describing specific [[countable set|countable]] [[ordinal number|ordinals]]. The smallest ones can be usefully and non-circularly expressed in terms of their [[Cantor normal form]]s. Beyond that, many ordinals of relevance to [[proof theory]] still have [[computable function|computable]] [[ordinal notation]]s (see [[ordinal analysis]]). However, it is not possible to decide effectively whether a given putative ordinal notation is a notation or not (for reasons somewhat analogous to the unsolvability of the [[halting problem]]); various more-concrete ways of defining ordinals that definitely have notations are available.

Since there are only countably many notations, all ordinals with notations are exhausted well below the [[first uncountable ordinal|first uncountable ordinal ω<sub>1</sub>]]; their [[supremum]] is called ''Church–Kleene'' ω<sub>1</sub> or ω{{su|b=1|p=CK}} (not to be confused with the first uncountable ordinal, ω<sub>1</sub>), described [[#The Church–Kleene ordinal|below]]. Ordinal numbers below ω{{su|b=1|p=CK}} are the ''recursive'' ordinals (see [[#Generalities on recursive ordinals|below]]). Countable ordinals larger than this may still be defined, but do not have notations.

Due to the focus on countable ordinals, [[ordinal arithmetic]] is used throughout, except where otherwise noted.  The ordinals described here are not as large as the ones described in [[large cardinals]], but they are large among those that have constructive notations (descriptions).  Larger and larger ordinals can be defined, but they become more and more difficult to describe.

== Generalities on recursive ordinals ==
{{Main|Computable ordinal}}

=== Ordinal notations ===

{{Main|Ordinal notation}}

[[Computable ordinal]]s (or recursive ordinals) are certain countable ordinals: loosely speaking those represented by a [[computable function]].  There are several equivalent definitions of this: the simplest is to say that a computable ordinal is the order-type of some recursive (i.e., computable) well-ordering of the [[Natural number|natural numbers]]; so, essentially, an ordinal is recursive when we can present the set of smaller ordinals in such a way that a computer ([[Turing machine]], say) can manipulate them (and, essentially, compare them).

<!-- Consider the following as a sort of stub for a yet-to-be-written article on "ordinal notations"... -->
A different definition uses [[Stephen Cole Kleene|Kleene]]'s system of [[ordinal notation]]s. Briefly, an ordinal notation is either the name zero (describing the ordinal 0), or the successor of an ordinal notation (describing the successor of the ordinal described by that notation), or a Turing machine (computable function) that produces an increasing sequence of ordinal notations (that describe the ordinal that is the limit of the sequence), and ordinal notations are (partially) ordered so as to make the successor of ''o'' greater than ''o'' and to make the limit greater than any term of the sequence (this order is computable; however, the set '''O''' of ordinal notations itself is highly non-recursive, owing to the impossibility of deciding whether a given Turing machine does indeed produce a sequence of notations); a recursive ordinal is then an ordinal described by some ordinal notation.

Any ordinal smaller than a recursive ordinal is itself recursive, so the set of all recursive ordinals forms a certain (countable) ordinal, the [[Church–Kleene ordinal]] (see below).

It is tempting to forget about ordinal notations, and only speak of the recursive ordinals themselves: and some statements are made about recursive ordinals which, in fact, concern the notations for these ordinals.  This leads to difficulties, however, as even the smallest infinite ordinal, ω, has many notations, some of which cannot be proved to be equivalent to the obvious notation (the simplest program that enumerates all natural numbers).

=== Relationship to systems of arithmetic ===

There is a relation between computable ordinals and certain [[formal system]]s (containing [[arithmetic]], that is, at least a reasonable fragment of [[Peano axioms|Peano arithmetic]]).

Certain computable ordinals are so large that while they can be given by a certain ordinal notation ''o'', a given formal system might not be sufficiently powerful to show that ''o'' is, indeed, an ordinal notation: the system does not show [[transfinite induction]] for such large ordinals.

For example, the usual [[First-order logic|first-order]] [[Peano axioms]] do not prove transfinite induction for (or beyond) [[epsilon numbers (mathematics)|ε<sub>0</sub>]]: while the ordinal ε<sub>0</sub> can easily be arithmetically described (it is countable), the Peano axioms are not strong enough to show that it is indeed an ordinal; in fact, transfinite induction on ε<sub>0</sub> proves the consistency of Peano's axioms (a theorem by [[Gerhard Gentzen|Gentzen]]), so by [[Gödel's second incompleteness theorem]], Peano's axioms cannot formalize that reasoning.  (This is at the basis of the [[Kirby–Paris theorem]] on [[Goodstein's theorem|Goodstein sequences]].)  Since Peano arithmetic ''can'' prove that any ordinal less than ε<sub>0</sub> is well ordered, we say that ε<sub>0</sub> measures the [[proof-theoretic strength]] of Peano's axioms.

But we can do this for systems far beyond Peano's axioms.  For example, the proof-theoretic strength of [[Kripke–Platek set theory]] is the [[Bachmann–Howard ordinal]], and, in fact, merely adding to Peano's axioms the axioms that state the well-ordering of all ordinals below the Bachmann–Howard ordinal is sufficient to obtain all arithmetical consequences of Kripke–Platek set theory.

== Specific recursive ordinals ==

=== Predicative definitions and the Veblen hierarchy ===
{{main|Veblen function}}
We have already mentioned (see  [[Ordinal arithmetic#Cantor normal form|Cantor normal form]]) the ordinal [[epsilon numbers (mathematics)|ε<sub>0</sub>]], which is the smallest satisfying the equation <math>\omega^\alpha = \alpha</math>, so it is the limit of the sequence 0, 1, <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega^\omega</math>, <math>\omega^{\omega^\omega}</math>, ...  The next ordinal satisfying this equation is called ε<sub>1</sub>: it is the limit of the sequence

:<math>\varepsilon_0+1, \qquad \omega^{\varepsilon_0+1}=\varepsilon_0\cdot\omega,\qquad\omega^{\omega^{\varepsilon_0+1}}=(\varepsilon_0)^\omega,\qquad\text{etc.}</math>

More generally, the <math>\iota</math>-th ordinal such that <math>\omega^\alpha = \alpha</math> is called <math>\varepsilon_\iota</math>.  We could define <math>\zeta_0</math> as the smallest ordinal such that <math>\varepsilon_\alpha=\alpha</math>, but since the Greek alphabet does not have transfinitely many letters it is better to use a more robust notation: define ordinals <math>\varphi_\gamma(\beta)</math> by transfinite induction as follows: let <math>\varphi_0(\beta) = \omega^\beta</math> and let <math>\varphi_{\gamma+1}(\beta)</math> be the <math>\beta</math>-th fixed point of <math>\varphi_\gamma</math> (i.e., the <math>\beta</math>-th ordinal such that <math>\varphi_\gamma(\alpha)=\alpha</math>; so for example, <math>\varphi_1(\beta) = \varepsilon_\beta</math>), and when <math>\delta</math> is a limit ordinal, define <math>\varphi_\delta(\alpha)</math> as the <math>\alpha</math>-th common fixed point of the <math>\varphi_\gamma</math> for all <math>\gamma<\delta</math>.  This family of functions is known as the ''[[Veblen hierarchy]]''  (there are inessential variations in the definition, such as letting, for <math>\delta</math> a limit ordinal, <math>\varphi_\delta(\alpha)</math> be the limit of the <math>\varphi_\gamma(\alpha)</math> for <math>\gamma<\delta</math>: this essentially just shifts the indices by 1, which is harmless). <math>\varphi_\gamma</math> is called the <math>\gamma^{th}</math> ''[[Veblen function]]'' (to the base <math>\omega</math>).

Ordering: <math>\varphi_\alpha(\beta) < \varphi_\gamma(\delta)</math> if and only if either (<math>\alpha = \gamma</math> and <math>\beta < \delta</math>) or (<math>\alpha < \gamma</math> and <math>\beta < \varphi_\gamma(\delta)</math>) or (<math>\alpha > \gamma</math> and <math>\varphi_\alpha(\beta) < \delta</math>).

=== The Feferman–Schütte ordinal and beyond ===

The smallest ordinal such that <math>\varphi_\alpha(0) = \alpha</math> is known as the [[Feferman–Schütte ordinal]] and generally written <math>\Gamma_0</math>.  It can be described as the set of all ordinals that can be written as finite expressions, starting from zero, using only the Veblen hierarchy and addition.  The Feferman–Schütte ordinal is important because, in a sense that is complicated to make precise, it is the smallest (infinite) ordinal that cannot be ("[[impredicative|predicatively]]") described using smaller ordinals.  It measures the strength of such systems as "[[Reverse mathematics#Arithmetical transfinite recursion ATR0|arithmetical transfinite recursion]]".

More generally, Γ<sub>''α''</sub> enumerates the ordinals that cannot be obtained from smaller ordinals using addition and the Veblen functions.

It is, of course, possible to describe ordinals beyond the Feferman–Schütte ordinal.  One could continue to seek fixed points in a more and more complicated manner: enumerate the fixed points of <math>\alpha\mapsto\Gamma_\alpha</math>, then enumerate the fixed points of ''that'', and so on, and then look for the first ordinal ''α'' such that ''α'' is obtained in ''α'' steps of this process, and continue diagonalizing in this ''ad hoc'' manner.  This leads to the definition of the "[[small Veblen ordinal|small]]" and "[[large Veblen ordinal|large]]" Veblen ordinals.

=== Impredicative ordinals ===
{{main|Ordinal collapsing function}}

To go far beyond the Feferman–Schütte ordinal, one needs to introduce new methods.  Unfortunately there is not yet any standard way to do this: every author in the subject seems to have invented their own system of notation, and it is quite hard to translate between the different systems. The first such system was introduced by [[Heinz Bachmann|Bachmann]] in 1950 (in an ''ad hoc'' manner), and different extensions and variations of it were described by Buchholz, [[Gaisi Takeuti|Takeuti]] (ordinal diagrams), [[Solomon Feferman|Feferman]] (θ systems), [[Peter Aczel|Aczel]], Bridge, [[Kurt Schütte|Schütte]], and Pohlers. However most systems use the same basic idea, of constructing new countable ordinals by using the existence of certain uncountable ordinals.  Here is an example of such a definition, described in much greater detail in the article on [[ordinal collapsing function]]:
*ψ(''α'') is defined to be the smallest ordinal that cannot be constructed by starting with 0, 1, ω and Ω, and repeatedly applying addition, multiplication and exponentiation, and ψ to previously constructed ordinals (except that ψ can only be applied to arguments  less than ''α'', to ensure that it is well defined).
Here Ω = ω<sub>1</sub> is the first uncountable ordinal. It is put in because otherwise the function ψ gets "stuck" at the smallest ordinal ''σ'' such that ε<sub>''σ''</sub>=''σ'': in particular ψ(''α'')=''σ'' for any ordinal α satisfying ''σ''≤''α''≤Ω. However the fact that we included Ω allows us to get past this point: ψ(Ω+1) is greater than ''σ''. The key property of Ω that we used is that it is greater than any ordinal produced by ψ.

To construct still larger ordinals, we can extend the definition of ψ by throwing in  more ways of constructing uncountable ordinals. There are several ways to do this, described to some extent in the article on [[ordinal collapsing function]].

The [[Bachmann–Howard ordinal]] (sometimes just called the Howard ordinal, ψ<sub>0</sub>(ε<sub>Ω+1</sub>) with the notation above) is an important one, because it describes the proof-theoretic strength of [[Kripke–Platek set theory]].  Indeed, the main importance of these large ordinals, and the reason to describe them, is their relation to certain formal systems as explained above.  However, such powerful formal systems as full [[second-order arithmetic]], let alone [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]], seem beyond reach for the moment.

=== Beyond even the Bachmann-Howard ordinal ===
Beyond this, there are multiple recursive ordinals which aren't as well known as the previous ones. The first of these is [[Ψ0(Ωω)|Buchholz's ordinal]], defined as <math>\psi_0(\Omega_\omega)</math>, abbreviated as just <math>\psi(\Omega_\omega)</math>, using the previous notation. It is the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\Pi_1^1-CA_0</math>,<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1986-01-01|title=A new system of proof-theoretic ordinal functions|journal=Annals of Pure and Applied Logic|language=en|volume=32|pages=195–207|doi=10.1016/0168-0072(86)90052-7|issn=0168-0072|last1=Buchholz |first1=W. |doi-access=free}}</ref> a first-order theory of arithmetic allowing quantification over the natural numbers as well as ''sets'' of natural numbers, and <math>ID_{<\omega}</math>, the "formal theory of finitely iterated inductive definitions".<ref>{{Cite book|last=Simpson|first=Stephen G.|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/subsystems-of-second-order-arithmetic/EA16CB4305831530B7015D6BC46B7424|title=Subsystems of Second Order Arithmetic|date=2009|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-88439-6|edition=2|series=Perspectives in Logic|location=Cambridge}}</ref>

Since the hydras from [[Buchholz hydra|Buchholz's hydra game]] are isomorphic to Buchholz's ordinal notation, the ordinals up to this point can be expressed using hydras from the game.<ref>W. Buchholz, "[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0168007287900789 An independence result for <math>(\Pi^1_1\mathsf{-CA})\mathsf{+BI}</math>]. (1987)"</ref><sup>p.136</sup> For example <math>+(0(\omega))</math> corresponds to <math>\psi(\Omega_\omega)</math>.

Next is the [[Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal|Takeuti-Feferman-Buchholz ordinal]], the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\Pi_1^1 -CA + BI</math>;<ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Buchholz | first1 = Wilfried
 | last2 = Feferman | first2 = Solomon | author2-link = Solomon Feferman
 | last3 = Pohlers | first3 = Wolfram
 | last4 = Sieg | first4 = Wilfried
 | doi = 10.1007/bfb0091894
 | isbn = 3-540-11170-0
 | mr = 655036
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag, Berlin-New York
 | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics
 | title = Iterated Inductive Definitions and Subsystems of Analysis: Recent Proof-Theoretical Studies
 | volume = 897
 | year = 1981}}</ref> and another subsystem of second-order arithmetic: <math>\Pi_1^1</math> - comprehension + transfinite induction, and <math>ID_\omega</math>, the "formal theory of <math>\omega</math>-times iterated inductive definitions".<ref name="Zoo">{{Cite web|date=2017-07-29|title=A Zoo of Ordinals|url=http://www.madore.org/~david/math/ordinal-zoo.pdf|access-date=2021-08-10|website=Madore}}</ref> In this notation, it is defined as <math>\psi_0(\varepsilon_{\Omega_\omega + 1})</math>. It is the supremum of the range of Buchholz's psi functions.<ref>W. Buchholz, [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0168007286900527 A new system of proof-theoretic ordinal functions] (1984) (lemmata 1.3 and 1.8). Accessed 2022-05-04.</ref> It was first named by David Madore.{{cn|date=May 2022}}

The next ordinal is mentioned in a piece of code describing [https://gist.github.com/AndrasKovacs/8d445c8457ea0967e807c726b2ce5a3a large countable ordinals and numbers in Agda], and defined by "AndrasKovacs" as <math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\omega+1} \cdot \varepsilon_0)</math>.

The next ordinal is mentioned in the same piece of code as earlier, and defined as <math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\omega^\omega})</math>. It is the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>ID_{<\omega^\omega}</math>. <!-- Once again, doesn't seem that significant or well-known, but still added it. Please add more information if you can find any. -->

This next ordinal is, once again, mentioned in this same piece of code, defined as <math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\varepsilon_0})</math>, is the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>ID_{<\varepsilon_0}</math>. In general, the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>ID_{<\nu}</math> is equal to <math>\psi_0(\Omega_{\nu})</math> — note that in this certain instance, <math>\Omega_0</math> represents <math>1</math>, the first nonzero ordinal.

Next is an unnamed ordinal, referred by David Madore as the "countable" collapse of <math>\varepsilon_{I+1}</math>,<ref name="Zoo" /> where <math>I</math> is the first [[inaccessible cardinal|inaccessible]] (=<math>\Pi^1_0</math>-indescribable) cardinal. This is the proof-theoretic ordinal of [[Kripke–Platek set theory|Kripke-Platek set theory]] augmented by the recursive inaccessibility of the class of ordinals (KPi), or, on the arithmetical side, of <math>\Delta^1_2</math> -comprehension + transfinite induction. Its value is equal to <math>\psi(\varepsilon_{I+1})</math> using an unknown function. 

Next is another unnamed ordinal, referred by David Madore as the "countable" collapse of <math>\varepsilon_{M+1}</math>,<ref name="Zoo" /> where <math>M</math> is the first [[Mahlo cardinal]]. This is the proof-theoretic ordinal of KPM, an extension of [[Kripke–Platek set theory|Kripke-Platek set theory]] based on a Mahlo cardinal.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rathjen|first=Michael|date=1994-01-01|title=Collapsing functions based on recursively large ordinals: A well-ordering proof for KPM|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01275469|journal=Archive for Mathematical Logic|language=en|volume=33|issue=1|pages=35–55|doi=10.1007/BF01275469|s2cid=35012853 |issn=1432-0665|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Its value is equal to <math>\psi(\varepsilon_{M+1})</math> using one of Buchholz's various psi functions.<ref>{{Cite web|date=1990|title=Ordinal notations based on a weakly Mahlo cardinal|url=https://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/Ord_Notation_Weakly_Mahlo.pdf|access-date=2021-08-10|website=University of Leeds}}</ref>

Next is another unnamed ordinal, referred by David Madore as the "countable" collapse of <math>\varepsilon_{K+1}</math>,<ref name="Zoo" /> where <math>K</math> is the first [[weakly compact cardinal|weakly compact]] (=<math>\Pi^1_1</math>-indescribable) cardinal. This is the proof-theoretic ordinal of [[Kripke–Platek set theory|Kripke-Platek set theory]] + Π3 - Ref. Its value is equal to <math>\Psi(\varepsilon_{K+1})</math> using Rathjen's Psi function.<ref>{{Cite web|date=1993-02-21|title=Proof Theory of Reflection|url=https://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/Ehab.pdf|access-date=2021-08-10|website=University of Leeds}}</ref> 

Next is another unnamed ordinal, referred by David Madore as the "countable" collapse of <math>\varepsilon_{\Xi+1}</math>,<ref name="Zoo" /> where <math>\Xi</math> is the first <math>\Pi^2_0</math>-indescribable cardinal.  This is the proof-theoretic ordinal of [[Kripke–Platek set theory|Kripke-Platek set theory]] + Πω-Ref. Its value is equal to <math>\Psi^{\varepsilon_{\Xi+1}}_X</math> using Stegert's Psi function, where <math>X</math> = (<math>\omega^+</math>; <math>P_0</math>; <math>\epsilon</math>, <math>\epsilon</math>, 0).<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Stegert|first=Jan-Carl|date=2010|title=Ordinal proof theory of Kripke-Platek set theory augmented by strong reflection principles|url=https://miami.uni-muenster.de/Record/429ac0b8-092f-426d-bf84-1e3a0adc8957|access-date=2021-08-10|website=miami.uni-muenster.de|language=English}}</ref> 

Next is the last unnamed ordinal, referred by David Madore as the proof-theoretic ordinal of Stability.<ref name="Zoo" /> This is the proof-theoretic ordinal of Stability, an extension of Kripke-Platek set theory. Its value is equal to <math>\Psi^{\varepsilon_{\Upsilon+1}}_X</math> using Stegert's Psi function, where <math>X</math> = (<math>\omega^+</math>; <math>P_0</math>; <math>\epsilon</math>, <math>\epsilon</math>, 0).<ref name=":2" /> 

Next is a group of ordinals about which not that much is known, but which are still fairly significant (in ascending order):

* The proof-theoretic ordinal of [[second-order arithmetic]].
* A possible limit of Taranovsky's C ordinal notation. (Conjectural, assuming well-foundedness of the notation system)
* The proof-theoretic ordinal of [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|ZFC]].

=== "Unrecursable" recursive ordinals ===

By dropping the requirement of having a concrete description, even larger recursive countable ordinals can be obtained as the ordinals measuring the strengths of various strong theories; roughly speaking, these ordinals are the smallest order types of "natural" ordinal notations that the theories cannot prove are well ordered. By taking stronger and stronger theories such as [[second-order arithmetic]], [[Zermelo set theory]], [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]], or Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with various [[large cardinal]] axioms, one gets some extremely large recursive ordinals.  (Strictly speaking it is not known that all of these really are ordinals: by construction, the ordinal strength of a theory can only be proved to be an ordinal from an even stronger theory.  So for the large cardinal axioms this becomes quite unclear.)

== Beyond recursive ordinals ==

<!-- This section should be much expanded, perhaps made into a separate article, because the present view is unbalanced: most of the article deals with recursive ordinals, and other large countable ordinals seem to be a kind of afterthought. -->

=== The Church–Kleene ordinal ===

The supremum of the set of [[recursive ordinal]]s is the smallest ordinal that ''cannot'' be described in a recursive way. (It is not the [[order type]] of any recursive well-ordering of the integers.) That ordinal is a countable ordinal called the [[Church–Kleene ordinal]], <math>\omega_1^{\mathrm{CK}}</math>. Thus, <math>\omega_1^{\mathrm{CK}}</math> is the smallest non-recursive ordinal, and there is no hope of precisely "describing" any ordinals from this point on&mdash;we can only ''define'' them. But it is still far less than the first uncountable ordinal, <math>\omega_1</math>. However, as its symbol suggests, it behaves in many ways rather like <math>\omega_1</math>. For instance, one can define ordinal collapsing functions using <math>\omega_1^{\mathrm{CK}}</math> instead of <math>\omega_1</math>.

=== Admissible ordinals ===
{{main|Admissible ordinal}}

The Church–Kleene ordinal is again related to [[Kripke–Platek set theory]], but now in a different way: whereas the Bachmann–Howard ordinal (described [[#Impredicative ordinals|above]]) was the smallest ordinal for which KP does not prove transfinite induction, the Church–Kleene ordinal is the smallest ''α'' such that the construction of the [[Constructible universe|Gödel universe]], ''L'', up to stage ''α'', yields a model <math>L_\alpha</math> of KP. Such ordinals are called ''admissible'', thus <math>\omega_1^{\mathrm{CK}}</math> is the smallest admissible ordinal (beyond ω in case the [[axiom of infinity]] is not included in KP).

By a theorem of [[Harvey Friedman (mathematician)|Friedman]], [[Ronald Jensen|Jensen]], and [[Gerald Sacks|Sacks]], the countable admissible ordinals are exactly those constructed in a manner similar to the Church–Kleene ordinal but for Turing machines with [[Oracle machine|oracles]].<ref>Friedman, H., Jensen, R. (1968). [https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079683 Note on admissible ordinals]. In: Barwise, J. (eds) The Syntax and Semantics of Infinitary Languages. Lecture Notes in Mathematics, vol 72. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg.</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Sacks | first1=Gerald E.
| title=Countable admissible ordinals and hyperdegrees
| journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]
| date=1976
| volume=20
| issue=2
| pages=213–262
| doi=10.1016/0001-8708(76)90187-0 | doi-access=free}}</ref> One sometimes writes <math>\omega_\alpha^{\mathrm{CK}}</math> for the <math>\alpha</math>-th ordinal that is either admissible or a limit of smaller admissibles.{{citation needed|date=May 2023}}

=== Beyond admissible ordinals ===
'''<math>\omega_\omega^{\mathrm{CK}}</math>''' is the smallest limit of admissible ordinals (mentioned later), yet the ordinal itself is not admissible. It is also the smallest <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>L_\alpha \cap P(\omega)</math> is a model of <math>\Pi^1_1</math>-comprehension.<ref name="Zoo" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|date=2006-02-07|title=Subsystems of Second-Order Arithmetic|url=https://www.personal.psu.edu/t20/sosoa/chapter1.pdf|access-date=2010-08-10|website=Penn State Institution}}</ref>

An ordinal that is both admissible and a limit of admissibles, or equivalently such that <math>\alpha</math> is the <math>\alpha</math>-th admissible ordinal, is called ''recursively inaccessible'', and the least recursively inaccessible may be denoted <math>\omega_1^{E_1}</math>.<ref>F. G. Abramson, G. E. Sacks, "[https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.101.3332&rep=rep1&type=pdf Uncountable Gandy Ordinals]" (1976), p.387. Accessed 13 February 2023.</ref> An ordinal that is both recursively inaccessible and a limit of recursively inaccessibles is called ''recursively hyperinaccessible''.<ref name="Zoo" /> There exists a theory of large ordinals in this manner that is highly parallel to that of (small) [[large cardinal property|large cardinals]].  For example, we can define ''recursively Mahlo ordinals'': these are the <math>\alpha</math> such that every <math>\alpha</math>-recursive closed unbounded subset of <math>\alpha</math> contains an admissible ordinal (a recursive analog of the definition of a [[Mahlo cardinal]]). The 1-section of Harrington's functional <math>{}^2S^\#</math> is equal to <math>L_\rho\cap\mathcal P(\omega)</math>, where <math>\rho</math> is the least recursively Mahlo ordinal.<ref name="Kechris1978">A. Kechris, "Spector Second-order Classes and Reflection". Appearing in ''Generalized Recursion Theory II: Proceedings of the 1977 Oslo Symposium'', Studies in Logic and the Foundation of Mathematics vol. 94 (1978), pp.147--183</ref><sup>p.171</sup>

But note that we are still talking about possibly countable ordinals here. (While the existence of inaccessible or Mahlo cardinals cannot be proved in [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]], that of recursively inaccessible or recursively Mahlo ordinals is a theorem of ZFC: in fact, any [[regular cardinal]] is recursively Mahlo and more, but even if we limit ourselves to countable ordinals,{{clarification needed|date=May 2023}} ZFC proves the existence of recursively Mahlo ordinals.  They are, however, beyond the reach of Kripke–Platek set theory.)

=== Reflection ===
For a set of formulae <math>\Gamma</math>, a limit ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called ''<math>\Gamma</math>-reflecting'' if the rank <math>L_\alpha</math> satisfies a certain reflection property for each <math>\Gamma</math>-formula <math>\phi</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv=1907.07611 |title=A Simplified Ordinal Analysis of First-Order Reflection |last1=Arai |first1=Toshiyasu |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |date=2019 |volume=85 |issue=3 |pages=1163–1185 |doi=10.1017/jsl.2020.23 }}</ref> These ordinals appear in ordinal analysis of theories such as ''KP+&Pi;<sub>3</sub>-ref'', a theory augmenting [[Kripke-Platek set theory]] by a <math>\Pi_3</math>-reflection schema. They can also be considered "recursive analogues" of some uncountable cardinals such as [[weakly compact cardinal|weakly compact cardinals]] and [[indescribable cardinal|indescribable cardinals]].<ref>W. Richter, P. Aczel, [https://www.duo.uio.no/handle/10852/44063 ''Inductive Definitions and Reflection Properties of Admissible Ordinals''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210126033604/https://www.duo.uio.no/handle/10852/44063 |date=2021-01-26 }} (1973)</ref> For example, an ordinal which <math>\Pi_3</math>-reflecting is called ''recursively weakly compact''.<ref name="RichterAczel74">{{Cite journal|date=1974-01-01|title=Inductive Definitions and Reflecting Properties of Admissible Ordinals|url=https://www.duo.uio.no/bitstream/handle/10852/44063/1973-13.pdf|journal=Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics|language=en|volume=79|pages=301–381|doi=10.1016/S0049-237X(08)70592-5|issn=0049-237X|last1=Richter |first1=Wayne |last2=Aczel |first2=Peter |hdl=10852/44063 |isbn=9780444105455 }}</ref> For finite <math>n</math>, the least <math>\Pi_n</math>-reflecting ordinal is also the supremum of the closure ordinals of monotonic inductive definitions whose graphs are [[Arithmetical hierarchy|Π<sub>m+1</sub><sup>0</sup>]]. <ref name="RichterAczel74" /><!--Pi_(m+1)^0 is a formula with only type-0 = number variables, see p.2-->

In particular, <math>\Pi_3</math>-reflecting ordinals also have a characterization using [[Higher-order function|higher-type functionals]] on ordinal functions, lending them the name ''2-admissible ordinals''. <ref name="RichterAczel74" /> An unpublished paper by [[Solomon Feferman]] supplies, for each finite <math>n</math>, a similar property corresponding to <math>\Pi_n</math>-reflection.<ref>S. Feferman, "[https://math.stanford.edu/~feferman/papers/Indes%20Cards%20&%20Admiss.pdf Indescribable Cardinals and Admissible Analogues]" (2013, unpublished). Accessed 18 November 2022.</ref>

=== Nonprojectibility ===
An admissible ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called ''nonprojectible'' if there is no total <math>\alpha</math>-recursive [[injective function]] mapping <math>\alpha</math> into a smaller ordinal.  (This is trivially true for regular cardinals; however, we are mainly interested in countable ordinals.)  Being nonprojectible is a much stronger condition than being admissible, recursively inaccessible, or even recursively Mahlo.<ref name=":3" /> By Jensen's method of projecta,<ref>K. J. Devlin, [https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/30905237.pdf An introduction to the fine structure of the constructible hierarchy], Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics (vol. 79, 1974). Accessed 2022-12-04.</ref> this statement is equivalent to the statement that the [[Constructible universe|Gödel universe]], ''L'', up to stage α, yields a model <math>L_\alpha</math> of KP + <math>\Sigma_1</math>-separation. However, <math>\Sigma_1</math>-separation on its own (not in the presence of <math>V=L</math>) is not a strong enough [[axiom schema]] to imply nonprojectibility, in fact there are transitive models of <math>KP</math>+<math>\Sigma_1</math>-separation of any countable admissible height <math> >\omega</math>.<ref>"Fred G. Abramson, [https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-symbolic-logic/article/abs/locally-countable-models-of-1separation/28D83F60A5B1D067E7726C464BD78A66 Locally countable models of <math>\Sigma_1</math>-separation]" (2014). Accessed 2022 July 23.</ref>

Nonprojectible ordinals are tied to [[Ronald Jensen|Jensen's]] work on projecta.<ref name="Zoo" /><ref>K. J. Devlin, [https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/30905237.pdf An introduction to the fine structure of the constructible hierarchy] (1974). Accessed 21 February 2023.</ref> The least ordinals that are nonprojectible relative to a given set are tied to Harrington's construction of the smallest reflecting Spector 2-class.<ref name="Kechris1978" /><sup>p.174</sup>

=== "Unprovable" ordinals ===
{{see also|Minimal model (set theory)}}
We can imagine even larger ordinals that are still countable. For example, if [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|ZFC]] has a [[transitive model]] (a hypothesis stronger than the mere hypothesis of consistency, and implied by the existence of an inaccessible cardinal), then there exists a countable <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>L_\alpha</math> is a model of ZFC.  Such ordinals are beyond the strength of ZFC in the sense that it cannot (by construction) prove their existence.

If <math>T</math> is a recursively enumerable set theory consistent with [[Axiom of constructibility|''V''=''L'']], then the least <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>(L_\alpha,\in)\vDash T</math> is less than the least stable ordinal, which follows.<ref>W. Marek, K. Rasmussen, {{WorldCat|oclc=1280819208|name=Spectrum of L}} ([https://eudml.org/doc/268487 EuDML] page), Państwowe Wydawn. Accessed 2022-12-01.</ref>
=== Stable ordinals ===
Even larger countable ordinals, called the ''stable ordinals'', can be defined by indescribability conditions or as those <math>\alpha</math> such that <math>L_\alpha</math> is a [[elementary equivalence|Σ<sub>1</sub>-elementary submodel]] of ''L''; the existence of these ordinals can be proved in ZFC,<ref>Barwise (1976), theorem 7.2.</ref> and they are closely related to the [[#Reflection_and_nonprojectibility|nonprojectible ordinal]]s from a model-theoretic perspective.<ref name="Zoo"/>{{rp|6}} For countable <math>\alpha</math>, stability of <math>\alpha</math> is equivalent to <math>L_\alpha\prec_{\Sigma_1}L_{\omega_1}</math>.<ref name="Zoo" />

The least stable level of <math>L</math> has some definability-related properties. Letting <math>\sigma</math> be least such that <math>L_\sigma\prec_1 L</math>:
* A set has a <math>\Sigma_1</math> definition in <math>L</math> iff it is a member of <math>L_\sigma</math>.<ref name="Zoo" /><sup>p.6</sup>
* A set <math>x\subseteq\mathbb N</math> is <math>\Delta^1_2</math> iff it is a member of <math>L_\sigma</math>.<ref name="Zoo" /><sup>p.6</sup>
* A set <math>x\subseteq\mathbb N</math> is <math>\Sigma^1_2</math> iff it is <math>\sigma</math>-recursively enumerable, in the terminology of [[alpha recursion theory]].<ref name="Zoo" /><sup>p.6</sup>

==== Variants of stable ordinals ====
These are weakened variants of stable ordinals. There are ordinals with these properties smaller than the aforementioned least nonprojectible ordinal,<ref name="Zoo"/> for example an ordinal is <math>(+1)</math>-stable iff it is <math>\Pi_n^0</math>-reflecting for all natural <math>n</math>.<ref name="RichterAczel74" />
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called <math>(+\beta)</math>-stable [[If and only if|iff]] <math>L_\alpha \prec_{\Sigma_1} L_{\alpha+\beta}</math><ref name="Zoo" />
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called <math>(^+)</math>-stable [[If and only if|iff]] <math>L_\alpha \prec_{\Sigma_1} L_{\beta}</math>, where <math>\beta</math> is the least [[admissible ordinal]] larger than <math>\alpha</math>.<ref name="Zoo" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|date=1978-01-01|title=Short Course on Admissible Recursion Theory|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0049237X08709418|journal=Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics|language=en|volume=94|pages=355–390|doi=10.1016/S0049-237X(08)70941-8|issn=0049-237X|last1=Simpson |first1=Stephen G. |isbn=9780444851635 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called <math>(^{++})</math>-stable [[If and only if|iff]] <math>L_\alpha \prec_{\Sigma_1} L_{\beta}</math>, where <math>\beta</math> is the least [[admissible ordinal]] larger than an admissible ordinal larger than <math>\alpha</math>.<ref name=":5" />
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called inaccessibly-stable [[If and only if|iff]] <math>L_\alpha \prec_{\Sigma_1} L_{\beta}</math>, where <math>\beta</math> is the least recursively inaccessible ordinal larger than <math>\alpha</math>.<ref name="Zoo" />
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called Mahlo-stable [[If and only if|iff]] <math>L_\alpha \prec_{\Sigma_1} L_{\beta}</math>, where <math>\beta</math> is the least recursively Mahlo ordinal larger than <math>\alpha</math>.<ref name="Zoo" />
* A countable ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is called doubly <math>(+1)</math>-stable [[If and only if|iff]] there is a <math>(+1)</math>-stable ordinal <math>\beta > \alpha</math> such that <math>L_\alpha \prec_{\Sigma_1} L_{\beta}</math>.<ref name="Zoo" />
Stronger weakenings of stability have appeared in proof-theoretic publications, including analysis of subsystems of [[second-order arithmetic]].<ref>{{Cite arXiv|last=Arai|first=Toshiyasu|eprint=1104.1842v1|title=Introducing the hardline in proof theory|date=1996|class=math.LO }}</ref>

== A pseudo-well-ordering ==
<!--{{Unreferenced section|date=December 2022}}-->
Within the [[Kleene's O|scheme of notations of Kleene]] some represent ordinals and some do not. One can define a recursive total ordering that is a subset of the Kleene notations and has an initial segment which is well-ordered with order-type <math>\omega_1^{\mathrm{CK}}</math>. Every recursively enumerable (or even hyperarithmetic) nonempty subset of this total ordering has a [[Greatest element and least element|least element]].  So it resembles a well-ordering in some respects.  For example, one can define the arithmetic operations on it.  Yet it is not possible to effectively determine exactly where the initial well-ordered part ends and the part lacking a least element begins.

For an example of a recursive pseudo-well-ordering, let S be [[Reverse_mathematics#Arithmetical_transfinite_recursion_ATR0|ATR<sub>0</sub>]] or another recursively axiomatizable theory that has an ω-model but no hyperarithmetical ω-models, and (if needed) conservatively extend S with [[Skolem function]]s.  Let T be the tree of (essentially) finite partial ω-models of S: A sequence of natural numbers <math>x_1,x_2,...,x_n</math> is in T iff S plus ∃m φ(m) ⇒ φ(x<sub>⌈φ⌉</sub>) (for the first n formulas φ with one numeric free variable; ⌈φ⌉ is the Gödel number) has no inconsistency proof shorter than n.  Then the [[Kleene–Brouwer order]] of T is a recursive pseudowellordering.

Any such construction must have order type <math>\omega_1^{CK}\times (1+\eta)+\rho</math>, where <math>\eta</math> is the order type of <math>(\mathbb Q,<)</math>, and <math>\rho</math> is a recursive ordinal. <ref>W. Chan, [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168007216301798 The countable admissible ordinal equivalence relation] (2017), p.1233. Accessed 28 December 2022.</ref>

==References==

Most books describing large countable ordinals are on proof theory, and unfortunately tend to be out of print.

===On recursive ordinals===
* [[Wolfram Pohlers]], ''Proof theory'', Springer 1989 {{isbn|0-387-51842-8}} (for Veblen hierarchy and some impredicative ordinals). This is probably the most readable book on large countable ordinals (which is not saying much).
* [[Gaisi Takeuti]], ''Proof theory'', 2nd edition 1987 {{isbn|0-444-10492-5}} (for ordinal diagrams)
* [[Kurt Schütte]], ''Proof theory'', Springer 1977 {{isbn|0-387-07911-4}} (for Veblen hierarchy and some impredicative ordinals)
* [[Craig Smorynski]], ''The varieties of arboreal experience'' Math. Intelligencer 4 (1982), no. 4, 182–189; contains an informal description of the Veblen hierarchy.
* [[Hartley Rogers Jr.]], ''Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability'' McGraw-Hill (1967) {{isbn|0-262-68052-1}} (describes recursive ordinals and the Church–Kleene ordinal)
* [[Larry W. Miller]], ''Normal Functions and Constructive Ordinal Notations'', ''[[The Journal of Symbolic Logic]]'', volume 41, number 2, June 1976, pages 439 to 459, {{JSTOR|2272243}},
* [[Hilbert Levitz]], ''[http://www.cs.fsu.edu/~levitz/ords.ps Transfinite Ordinals and Their Notations: For The Uninitiated]'', expository article (8 pages, in [[PostScript]])
* [[Herman Ruge Jervell]], [https://www.uio.no/studier/emner/matnat/ifi/INF5800/v11/undervisningsmateriale/hrj-TruthProvability.pdf Truth and provability], manuscript in progress.
